prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 (analog resistive) using an MCP3008 ADC connected on the SPI0 hardware bus, with CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM); the sensor’s analog output is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0), and the program must sample once per second, logging the raw 10‑bit ADC value (0‑1023) to the console together with a timestamp, while providing robust error handling for any SPI initialization or transfer failures, ensuring that the SPI handle is closed and the driver library is terminated cleanly on all exit paths, and supporting graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the current from an MLX91219 Hall‑Effect Current Sensor (analog output) using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1, with the sensor’s ADDR pin tied to GND, the sensor’s analog output connected to ADS1115 channel AIN0, SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); configure the ADS1115 for single‑shot mode, single‑ended input on AIN0 (MUX = 100), a programmable gain of ±4.096 V and a data rate of 128 SPS, then every 500 ms read the 16‑bit conversion result using the appropriate API call with correct byte order, convert it to amperes, and log the current value to the console, while gracefully handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO4 (BCM) and routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) while using the MCP3008 chip‑enable CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver, verify successful SPI open and transfer operations, and on each one‑second interval log a timestamped CSV row containing the current time, a boolean flame‑detected flag derived from the digital line, and an approximated temperature calculated from the analog reading to a file named flame_data.csv, while handling errors by skipping the entry and printing a diagnostic message if the sensor is absent or any SPI or file operation fails, and must ensure all resources are cleanly released on normal exit or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) as a digital input and an LM393‑based Heat Sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 on I2C bus 1 using channel AIN0 (single‑ended), polling both every 100 ms with a 50 ms debounce applied to the flame sensor, and activates an active‑HIGH buzzer on GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds when both sensors indicate a fire condition at the same time; the program must log a fire event with a timestamp to a file named fire_log.txt when both conditions trigger, log “Flame detected!” if only the flame sensor is active, and log the temperature reading if only the temperature exceeds 60 °C, while performing thorough error handling that checks driver library initialization, I2C opening, ADC configuration writes, ADC reads, and log file creation, printing descriptive error messages to stderr for any failure, releasing any resources acquired so far and exiting with code 1 on any initialization error, and, if an ADC read fails due to I2C error or missing sensor, logging the error and continuing without crashing; the application should handle SIGINT by clearing a running flag so the main loop exits cleanly, and on exit it must turn off the buzzer, deregister any interrupt service routine, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and invoke the driver library’s cleanup call, using only the provided driver library (no other libraries), driving the buzzer with a simple digital write (no PWM), and compiling without warnings under gcc ‑Wall with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the Melexis MLX91219 current sensor (SOIC‑8, –40 °C to 125 °C) through an external MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0 (spidev0.0) configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, sampling once per second, logs each reading with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named current_log.txt, and drives a cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) HIGH when the measured current exceeds a defined threshold and LOW otherwise; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, read and write call, detect SPI transfer failures, and treat ADC values of all‑zero or all‑ones as a sensor‑absent condition, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must close the SPI file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, and ensure the fan is turned OFF, using the appropriate driver interface for all GPIO control, opening the GPIO chip by name and attempting the Pi 5 specific API call before falling back to chip 0, and include stdint.h along with any other required standard headers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a Honeywell/SGX MICROceL MICS-4514 CO sensor (dual‑element MOS, NO2/CO) via I2C bus 1, using an external 16‑bit ADC such as an ADS1115 or a simulated 16‑bit raw reading, converts the raw CO resistance value to a concentration in ppm with a calibrated logarithmic curve, and logs each timestamped ppm value to a file named co_log.txt every 5 seconds; the program must verify successful driver library initialization, creation of the I2C handle, and detect any I2C read failures that indicate a missing sensor or bus error, and it must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the digital output (DO) of a KY‑038 sound sensor module on a single‑bit GPIO bus, using the sensor’s DO pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), and prints the sound level reading (0 or 1) to the console each loop iteration with a 100 ms delay between reads; when the sensor reports a sound event—remembering that the KY‑038 DO pin goes LOW when the detected sound exceeds the onboard potentiometer threshold—the program must trigger an alarm LED attached to GPIO18 (BCM) by turning the LED on for 1 s and then off, and continue monitoring; the implementation must verify successful initialization of the GPIO driver, successful opening of the chip, successful line request, and must check the result of every I/O operation, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully by printing an error message and exiting; finally, the program must catch SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) or SIGTERM and cleanly release all GPIO lines before exiting, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors the SW‑420 vibration sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) via the /dev/gpiochip0 GPIO character device, requesting the single line with the consumer label “vibration‑monitor” and configuring it for falling‑edge detection because the sensor’s DO output is active‑low, open‑collector (idle HIGH, pulls LOW when vibration exceeds the threshold). prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads the Texas Instruments OPT3101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, logging every 500 ms the distance measurement from channel 0, the ambient light value, and any error flags to the console, while implementing robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as a missing sensor or bus errors and guaranteeing that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the trigger output and GPIO 18 (BCM) as the echo input, issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse each cycle, waiting up to 200 ms for the echo rising edge and up to 200 ms for the echo falling edge, and performing one read per second; each valid measurement must be logged to the console together with a timestamp, while the code must handle driver library initialization failure, echo‑edge timeouts, and invalid pulse durations (≤ 0 µs or > 38 ms, the HC‑SR04 maximum range timeout), include a comment noting that the HC‑SR04 operates at 5 V and the Pi GPIO is only 3.3 V tolerant and therefore a 1 kΩ resistor must be used on the echo line within the library’s API call() that provides microsecond precision, and finally ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads a range profile from a Texas Instruments IWR1443 mmWave radar over UART (/dev/serial0), decodes each data frame marked by an 8‑byte magic word header followed by 128 bytes of raw range profile data representing 64 little‑endian 16‑bit distance bins, checks whether any bin indicates a target within a 1.0‑meter distance threshold, and on detection logs an intrusion entry containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the distance in meters to a comma‑separated file named intrusion_log.csv, while also activating an alert LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds; the program must handle UART initialization errors using the POSIX driver library, validate all I/O operations, gracefully manage sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensure clean release of all resources on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads obstacle detection data from an E18-D80NK IR sensor connected to GPIO 17, where the sensor presents an active‑low signal (0 when an obstacle is within the threshold distance and 1 otherwise), and drives a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active‑high) such that the buzzer is activated whenever an obstacle is detected and deactivated when the obstacle is removed; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms via the GPIO bus, log each state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named obstacle_log.txt, rigorously check all driver return values and handle any errors such as chip open failure, line request failure, or read/write errors, and also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and closes the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK Chirp ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the distance measurement every 100 ms, logs each distance together with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt, and monitors the reading so that when the measured distance falls below 10.0 cm the program asserts a GPIO alert on physical pin 17 (BCM 17); the implementation must handle all I2C read/write errors, detect the absence of the sensor, and manage any errors that occur while creating or writing the log file, and it must also cleanly release all resources—including I2C handles, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—when receiving a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a parking‑assistance system using the STMicroelectronics VL53L1X Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms in the main loop, check the return code of every driver, I2C, and file operation, and for each measurement append a line “timestamp,distance_mm” to a file named distance_log.csv, creating the file with a header row “timestamp,distance_mm” only when it does not already exist, while also printing a parking guidance message to stdout based on the measured distance—‘STOP’ for less than 300 mm, ‘APPROACH’ for 300‑600 mm, ‘SLOW’ for 600‑1200 mm, and ‘CLEAR’ for greater than 1200 mm; the application must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and de‑initialises the sensor driver on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense CH201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) every 100 ms, logs each timestamped distance and the corresponding LED blink frequency to stdout, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 18 (BCM) through a 330 Ω current‑limiting resistor to 3.3 V so that the LED blinks faster as the measured distance decreases, with each loop iteration performing exactly one half‑cycle of the LED blink (on or off) to keep the blinking smooth across samples; the program must check every driver and I2C call, retry any failed I2C read or write up to three times with 10 ms delays, and gracefully handle sensor‑absent conditions (I2C open failure) and bus‑error paths, and it must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that on termination cleanly close the I2C handle, turn off the LED, and shut down the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at a 100 ms sampling interval, triggering each measurement with the required write command, waiting the appropriate delay, then reading the 2‑byte distance value in centimeters, and appending each reading to a comma‑separated file named distance_log.csv formatted as “timestamp,distance_cm”; the program must include robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, or read/write timeouts, implement retry logic for transient errors, log any errors to stderr, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two TCRT5000 IR obstacle avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 27 (physical pin 13, BCM), polls each sensor every 10 ms, applies a 50 ms software debounce per sensor, and logs every state transition to a file named proximity_log.txt with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the sensor ID (1 or 2), and the event type ('DETECTED' for a HIGH‑to‑LOW transition indicating an obstacle and 'CLEARED' for a LOW‑to‑HIGH transition indicating clearance); the program must check the return values of the library’s API call() three times as required, verify all file I/O operations, and on all exit paths—including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM—ensure clean resource release by closing the log file and calling the library’s API call() to release the GPIO resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously measures distance from a TDK CH‑101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c‑1) by opening the I2C device with open(2), setting the slave address with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), and using a helper that performs a combined write‑then‑read transaction to poll the MEAS_STATUS register with a 50 ms timeout before reading a successful distance measurement; after each successful read the program must wait 500 ms before the next sample, log an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the distance in millimetres to a CSV file named “distance_log.csv” with columns timestamp,distance_mm, checking the result of every open, ioctl, read, write and fopen call and, on any I2C failure, printing a diagnostic message including errno to stderr and skipping that sample without crashing; the application must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close the I2C file descriptor, flush and close the CSV file, and then exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads zone distance data from a VL53L5CX ToF sensor connected on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1), configures the sensor for an 8×8 zone grid (64 zones), and logs all 64 zone distances to the console every 500 ms; the implementation must perform all I2C register reads and writes manually using standard Linux file I/O without any external driver library, include robust error handling for both I2C communication and sensor initialization, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling of SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads distance measurements from a Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling the distance every 100 ms and logging each measurement to the console together with a millisecond timestamp; the implementation must check the return values of all driver initialization and I2C read/write calls, retry any failed I2C transaction up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts, and gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, while also ensuring that on all exit paths—including a graceful shutdown triggered by SIGINT (Ctrl‑C)—the I2C handle is closed and the driver library is properly terminated.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a capacitive touch‑based proximity detector using an MPR121 connected on I2C bus 1, reads the device ID to verify the sensor is present, configures all required MPR121 registers including FFI, SFI, ESI, debounce, AFE configuration and baseline filtering, monitors the touch inputs for a proximity event, and when such an event is detected turns an LED wired to GPIO 27 (BCM numbering) on for exactly one second, logs the proximity event with a timestamp to a file named proximity.log, handles any I2C communication errors gracefully, and ensures that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that measures distance using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus with the trigger line wired to GPIO17 (BCM, output) and the echo line to GPIO18 (BCM, input); the program must hold the trigger low for 5 µs, then pulse it high for 10 µs before returning it low, wait up to 30 ms for the echo rising edge, then measure the echo pulse width with a further 30 ms timeout, compute distance using the speed of sound ≈ 343 m/s at 20 °C, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range and log an error line instead, and otherwise write a line to a file named distance_log.txt every second containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the measured distance, flushing after each write; each access to the trigger and echo pins must include proper error checking, sensor‑absent conditions (echo never rises) and timeout paths must be handled explicitly, a SIGINT handler must be installed that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must release all driver resources, close the log file and exit cleanly without leaking resources on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that measures distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor using an interrupt‑driven echo pulse‑width measurement on the GPIO bus, with TRIG connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and ECHO connected to GPIO18 (BCM) through a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider to keep the Pi input at ~3.3 V, generating a 10 µs trigger pulse once per second, capturing the echo pulse width via an ISR callback on either‑edge transitions, validating that the pulse width is greater than zero and falls within a sane range (approximately 58 µs to 25 ms, corresponding to about 1 cm to 4 m) while handling tick wrap‑around, converting the measured time to meters, and appending each reading together with a timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt; the program must check that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file opens successfully, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly shuts down by disabling the ISR, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call, with no use of UDP networking or any other external communication.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, controls the sensor’s XSHUT pin with GPIO27 (BCM) configured as an output and set high to enable the sensor (active‑low trigger), repeatedly reads the distance every 100 ms, and logs each reading to the systemd journal via syslog including a timestamp, the measured distance in millimetres, and the sensor status, using LOG_INFO for successful reads and LOG_ERR for any read failures; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the I2C device can be opened, handle read errors by logging them and continuing the loop without crashing, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C handle, terminate the driver library, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to poll distance measurements every 100 ms, converts the 16‑bit register value from millimetres to centimetres, and controls a gate actuator connected to GPIO24 (BCM, active‑high) so that the gate is opened when the measured distance is less than 20 cm and closed otherwise, initializing the gate to the closed state (GPIO24 low) at startup; the program must log each distance reading, each gate state change, and any errors with timestamps to a file named “gate_log.txt”, perform error handling for all I2C operations, sensor initialization, and file operations, and include a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that gracefully shuts down by closing the I2C interface, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that measures distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor using an interrupt‑driven echo timing callback and pans an SG90 servo motor via the library’s API call to track it, logging timestamp, distance in centimeters, and the API call angle in degrees to a file named distance_log.csv with a header row and flushing after each write; the HC‑SR04 trigger pin is connected to GPIO23 (BCM) and must be pulsed high for 10 µs every 100 ms, the echo pin is on GPIO24 (BCM) and must be timed with a 30 ms timeout using the 32‑bit tick counter with wrap‑around handling, while the SG90 servo is driven from GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM‑capable) and its angle is set through the API call; the program must check driver initialization, alert registration, API call return codes, and file opening, and on an invalid distance reading (out of the 2‑400 cm range or no echo) it must log –1.0 and command the servo to 90 degrees; distance readings are to be filtered with a 5‑sample moving average, and the shared pulse‑width data between the interrupt callback and the main loop must be protected by a flag‑based handshake where the callback sets pulse_width and a new_pulse flag and the main thread reads and clears it; a volatile sig_atomic_t flag must be used to catch SIGINT, upon which the program stops the servo by issuing the API call with 0, closes the CSV file, and calls the API cleanup function before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that communicates with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reads a distance measurement every 50 ms, stores each reading in millimetres in a circular buffer holding the last ten values, and drives a warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) high whenever a reading falls below 200 mm and low otherwise; the implementation must follow the recommended STMicroelectronics initialization sequence—set the default configuration, enable signal‑rate checking, configure cross‑talk compensation, and start ranging—while checking every I2C read and write for errors, handling sensor initialization failures, printing any read error and continuing operation, and providing a SIGINT handler that cleanly shuts down by turning off the LED, closing the I2C interface, terminating the driver usage, and releasing all resources on any exit path, using only modern APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1102 proximity sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, configures the sensor’s proximity interrupt to GPIO27 (BCM numbering) on a rising edge, and on each interrupt reads the 16‑bit proximity value, compares it to a threshold (default 1000 but overrideable with a command‑line option “‑t <threshold>”), and appends a line to a file named proximity.log containing the current timestamp in “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” format, the raw proximity reading, and the status string “SAFE” if the value is less than or equal to the threshold or “ALERT” if it exceeds the threshold; the program must also accept an optional “‑a <i2c_address>” argument to set the I2C address in hex or decimal, must initialise the I2C interface and GPIO with full error checking, must verify every I2C transaction, GPIO setup, and file operation and print any errors to stderr, must implement a thread‑safe interrupt handler that does not perform blocking calls (using a flag or queue to defer processing), and must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly shuts down by closing the I2C device, closing the log file, and terminating the sensor driver, while using the provided driver facilities for GPIO and I2C but not for higher‑level sensor handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor and drives an 8‑ohm speaker as a theremin‑like instrument, using the hardware‑timed PWM on PWM0 (GPIO18, BCM) to generate audio tones whose pitch is controlled by the measured distance; the HC‑SR04 trigger line must be pulsed for 10 µs on GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line read on GPIO24 (BCM) with a timeout of 200 ms, mapping distances from 2 cm to 200 cm to frequencies between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz on a logarithmic scale with a 50 % duty cycle, while performing robust error checking on every driver API call and, if a distance is out of range or a timeout occurs, preserving the previous frequency, and installing a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops the PWM and terminates the driver, ensuring all resources are released on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that synthesizes a theremin‑like instrument using a piezo buzzer whose pitch is controlled by the distance measured with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor; the buzzer is connected to PWM0 on GPIO18 (BCM), the HC‑SR04 trigger line to GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line to GPIO24 (BCM) with a pull‑down resistor, and the program must initialize the driver library, verify that the GPIO modes are correctly set, then in a loop trigger the sensor with a low‑initial state followed by a 10 µs high pulse, measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using the library’s timing API, enforce an echo timeout of 100 ms (reporting an error and reusing the last valid distance if exceeded), wait 10 ms between readings, map the practical distance range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a frequency range of 200 Hz to 2000 Hz (clamping outside values), generate a continuous tone on the buzzer using the library’s frequency generation API (not raw PWM), print both the measured distance and the resulting frequency to the console each iteration, handle any sensor read failures gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM and shuts down the driver library cleanly on program termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously measures the distance to the nearest object using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor, triggering the sensor on GPIO17 (BCM) with a 10 µs pulse and reading the echo on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 50 ms timeout, looping every 500 ms; the program must initialise the driver library, configure the trigger pin as an output initially low and the echo pin as an input, check that the driver library initialisation succeeds, obtain each echo pulse duration, convert it to a distance in centimeters, reject any reading below 2 cm or above 400 cm and print “Invalid reading” for those, otherwise print the valid distance as “Distance: X.XX cm”, and if the distance is below 10 cm also print “Too close!”; it must handle a timeout from the echo measurement by treating it as a –1 result, and it must install a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, then terminates the driver library and releases all resources before exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor over SPI (mode 0, 1 MHz clock) using the chip‑select line on GPIO8 (BCM, CE0), continuously reads the distance for an obstacle‑avoidance application with a 100 ms delay between readings, and appends each timestamp and distance value in millimetres (range 200‑5000 mm) to a file named distance_log.csv opened in append mode; the program must use the sensor driver’s API call for SPI read operations, handle SPI communication errors, sensor initialization failures, and sensor‑absent conditions gracefully by logging errors to stderr while continuing to run indefinitely, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the SPI handle, releases all resources, and flushes and closes the CSV log file on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1175 ambient light and proximity sensor over I2C using the documented default address, samples the ambient light value every 5 seconds, and appends each reading to a file named proximity_log.csv with a header row “timestamp,als_visible” where the timestamp is formatted in ISO‑8601; the implementation must check the result of every I2C open, read, and write call, handle the cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and ensure that on all exit paths—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—the I2C file descriptor and the log file are cleanly closed, while using only standard POSIX/Linux APIs and including <stdint.h> for the uint8_t/uint16_t types.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously measures the distance to an object with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected with the trigger line on GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line on GPIO24 (BCM), issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse and waiting up to a 50 ms timeout for both the rising and falling edges, then pausing 100 ms before the next measurement, and maps the measured distance (valid from 2 cm to 400 cm) to a servo angle using an SG90 servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM, powered from 5 V with a common ground) by calling the provided API to set pulse widths of 500 µs for 0° and 2500 µs for 180°, where distances below 20 cm correspond to 0°, distances above 200 cm correspond to 180°, and intermediate values are linearly interpolated; each cycle the program must print the distance and the corresponding angle, initialise the driver with error checking and exit with a clear message if initialisation fails, verify the return of every API call, treat a timeout from the sensor as a distance of –1.0, guard against division by zero or invalid angles, and install a SIGINT handler that stops the servo by sending a 0‑degree command through the API and cleanly shuts down the driver before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si7005 humidity and temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented device address, verifies successful initialization of the driver library and opening of the I2C bus, and then repeatedly reads the sensor by first writing the CONFIG register, waiting 10 ms, writing the register address to be read, waiting another 10 ms for conversion, and finally performing the I2C read; each successful read must be logged to the console every 2 seconds, while every I2C read or write operation must be checked for errors and, on any failure, the program must close and re‑open the I2C handle to attempt recovery, and the application must handle SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle and terminates the driver library on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads raw accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense MPU‑6050 over I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2 BCM, SCL on GPIO3 BCM) and logs it to the console, beginning with a brief startup message and ending with a clean‑shutdown message; the program must first verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register, then every 100 ms read the 14‑byte data block starting at the documented register using the library’s API call, parse the big‑endian int16 values for the three‑axis accelerometer, temperature and three‑axis gyroscope, and print those values to stdout each cycle, while handling any I2C read/write errors or sensor‑absent conditions, and must catch SIGINT or SIGTERM to close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s API call for cleanup before exiting.

int read_sht40(int handle, float *temperature, float *humidity) {
    char buffer[6];

        fprintf(stderr, "CRC check failed\n");
        return -1;
    }

    // Convert data to temperature and humidity
    *temperature = (float)buffer[3] * 256.0 + (float)buffer[4];
    *humidity = (float)buffer[5] * 256.0;

    return 0;
}

int validate_crc8(uint8_t data) {
    uint8_t crc = 0xFF;
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {

        for (int j = 0; j < 8; j++) {
            if (crc & 0x80) {

            } else {
                crc <<= 1;
            }
        }
    }
    return crc == data;
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors air‑duct pressure in a simulated HVAC system using the Sensirion SDP810‑500Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting at least 50 ms, then reading the 9‑byte result (2 bytes pressure, 1 byte CRC, 2 bytes temperature, 1 byte CRC, 3 bytes scale factor) once per second, validating every I2C read and write as well as each CRC‑8 using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor, logging each successful sample to a file named hvac_pressure_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C, and on any I2C or CRC error writing an error line with the timestamp and continuing, checking the return of every initialization call (the two required library API calls and fopen) and exiting with an error message if any fails, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and calling the library’s cleanup API function before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that drives a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C, buffers CO₂, temperature and humidity readings in a thread‑safe circular buffer of capacity 100, and periodically persists the data to a timestamped CSV file in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if it does not exist) with a header row, while logging any errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log; the main loop must wait at least one second after issuing the start‑periodic‑measurement command before the first read, then read the sensor every five seconds, validating the CRC‑8 of each value using the polynomial and initial value documented for the device and, on any CRC failure or I2C read/write error, log the error and skip that reading; a separate logging thread must write the buffered records to the CSV file every sixty seconds, and the program must handle SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag to stop the main loop, send the documented stop‑periodic‑measurement command, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffered data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle and cleanly terminate the driver without any resource leaks.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature, humidity and pressure from a BME280 sensor attached to I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL, device file /dev/i2c-1) using the documented I2C address, verifies that the BME280 chip ID matches the documented value during initialization, and then logs a line to a file named bme280_log.csv every five seconds containing a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, the temperature in degrees Celsius, the relative humidity in percent, and the pressure in hectopascals; the program must check the result of every I2C read and write system call, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and ensure that all file descriptors and file pointers are cleanly released on any exit path, including when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, employing the library's API call for I2C communication and the library's API call for a hardware timer that triggers every 50 ms; each reading must be stored in a circular buffer sized to hold timestamped pressure values for the last 60 seconds, from which a rolling average is computed, and if the current pressure deviates by more than 5 hPa from that average the program shall assert an active‑HIGH alert on GPIO24, logging the alert to stderr, while also logging any I2C failures or sensor absence with robust error handling; the sampling loop must use the library's API call for the 50 ms timer, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must cleanly release resources by closing the I2C interface, resetting GPIO24, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that configures I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 pressure sensor, validates the calibration data read from the documented registers before any measurement, and then uses a hardware timer interrupt to trigger a sample every 500 ms, reading temperature in degrees Celsius and pressure in pascals with the oversampling setting set to 0 (ultra low power) and appending the results to a file named bmp180_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for all I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the CPU temperature from the thermal zone file /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, maps the temperature linearly to a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 25 kHz frequency and a 0‑255 range such that 40 °C corresponds to 0 % duty, 70 °C to 100 % duty and values are clamped below 40 °C and above 70 °C, drives a PWM‑controlled cooling fan accordingly, logs every 5 seconds to a file named fan_log.txt the current timestamp, temperature and duty cycle, and includes robust error handling for failures to read the temperature, write to the log file, or initialize the PWM driver, while also installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully stop the fan, close any open files and terminate the PWM driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the temperature from an LM75 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs the read once per second, stores each reading in an in‑memory circular buffer of capacity 60 samples protected by a mutex, updates a running average from the buffer, and drives an alert LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) from a background thread so that the LED is turned on whenever the temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the implementation must check the result of every I2C read/write and every GPIO initialization call, log any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions to stderr, attempt to re‑initialize the hardware on such errors, and ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, error paths, and receipt of SIGINT—the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and destroying the mutex.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 OUT to GPIO23 (BCM), sensor 2 OUT to GPIO24 (BCM), and driving an LED (anode) on GPIO25 (BCM) through a 220‑330 Ω resistor to ground, polling the sensor outputs every 100 ms, turning the LED on immediately when either sensor reads LOW (active‑LOW indicating an obstacle within roughly 10 cm) and turning it off only when both sensors read HIGH, verifying the driver initialization and checking the return code of every library API call, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released via the appropriate library call on every exit path, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a conveyor belt using two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected via GPIO, with sensor 1 OUT wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 OUT wired to GPIO18 (BCM); the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, validate each sensor read, and consider a stall confirmed only when both sensors read LOW (0) continuously for at least 2 seconds, then record a timestamped entry for each confirmed stall in a file named stall_log.txt while avoiding duplicate entries for the same stall event, handling any file I/O errors that may occur, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the process receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with the Texas Instruments TMAG5170‑Q1 I2C 3D Hall‑Effect sensor on I2C bus 1, configures the sensor for continuous‑conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range, then reads the X, Y, and Z magnetic field values every 100 ms in an infinite loop until the user terminates the program with Ctrl‑C, logging each reading to a CSV file named magnetic_log.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and writing a header row if the file is newly created, while checking every I2C read and write return code and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions by printing error messages to stderr and continuing operation, and finally registering a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the CSV file, and invoking the sensor’s library cleanup call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that runs as a daemon and continuously polls the SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to the GPIO bus on pin GPIO23 (BCM numbering), using a pull‑down resistor on the input to keep the line low when dry, reading the sensor every 2 seconds and generating an alert whenever a logic HIGH is detected; on each detection the program must print an alert message to stdout and append a line to a file named flood_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected”, while also checking that the driver library initializes correctly and, if a GPIO read fails, logging an error entry to the same file and scheduling an automatic re‑initialization attempt after 60 seconds; the daemon must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to release all resources cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Bookworm or later that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall‑effect sensor connected to the GPIO bus, with the sensor output wired to physical pin 7 (BCM GPIO4), by configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled and counting rising‑edge pulses using GPIO interrupts; the program must count pulses in a one‑second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, compute the revolutions per minute, and log one sample per second to a file named rpm_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>” while also printing the same line to stdout, flushing the file after each write; it must check every driver‑library call and the file‑open call for errors, exiting with a diagnostic message on failure, but if the sensor is absent or not rotating it should log an RPM of 0 instead of aborting; finally, the program must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall‑effect sensors connected on the GPIO bus in an interrupt‑driven quadrature configuration, with Sensor A wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Sensor B to GPIO27 (BCM) and hardware pull‑up resistors providing the required 90° electrical offset, to detect the direction of rotation and log each clockwise or counter‑clockwise event to a file named rotation_log.txt using millisecond‑precision timestamps formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm”; the implementation must employ the driver’s edge‑triggered alerts via the library’s API call for interrupt handling (without using any other driver library), maintain a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to infer direction, protect the shared state between the ISR and the main thread with a mutex, have the main loop wait on a condition variable or sleep rather than busy‑wait, check all error paths including each of the three library’s API call() invocations and the file open operation, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by flushing and closing the log file and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the SparkFun ADXL345 I2C accelerometer on I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1, wiring the ADXL345 INT1 pin to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering), to detect free‑fall events via a GPIO interrupt, verify the device ID at startup (ensuring the documented value is read), place the sensor in standby mode before any register writes, and on each interrupt capture timestamped acceleration samples (X, Y, Z) only while free‑fall is active, writing them to a file named freefall_log.csv that is created with a header row and uses the format YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm,X,Y,Z with the file flushed after each write; the implementation must check every I2C system call and GPIO operation for errors, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, run a poll‑based loop on the driver’s event file descriptor (no threads), and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly disable the sensor’s interrupts, close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO line, close the sensor device, and close the CSV log file.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR IMU over I2C bus 1 using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM) at a 104 Hz output data rate, logs each timestamped reading to a CSV file named motion_log.txt, and implements a basic fall‑detection state machine that transitions from IDLE to FREEFALL when the acceleration magnitude falls below 0.2 g and then to IMPACT when it exceeds 2.5 g within a 1.0 s detection window, while handling I2C read/write errors, sensor‑absent conditions verified by a WHO_AM_I check, and other bus errors gracefully, and ensures clean resource release on SIGINT or SIGTERM; the sensor must be configured for a ±2 g accelerometer range and a ±250 dps gyroscope range.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the digital output (DO) of a KY-026 Flame Sensor Module connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) on the GPIO bus every 500 ms, enables the internal pull‑up resistor on that line because the sensor’s open‑collector output is active‑LOW (LOW indicates flame, HIGH indicates no flame), and writes each reading to an append‑mode file named flame_events.log with an immediately flushed line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS – Flame detected: YES” when the pin reads LOW or “… NO” when it reads HIGH; when a flame is detected the program must also print the message “FLAME DETECTED!” to the console, and it must check that the driver initialization succeeded, verify that the log file handle is valid, and treat any sensor read error (e.g., the API returning PI_BAD_GPIO) by logging an error line instead of a false positive; a SIGINT handler should be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C sets a flag that cleanly exits the polling loop, and on any exit path the program must close the log file if open and call the library’s cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads acceleration data from an Omron D7S‑0001 vibration sensor over the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, samples the X, Y, and Z axes every 100 ms, and appends each sample to a file named vibration_log.csv with a header line “Timestamp,X,Y,Z” where the timestamp is an ISO‑8601 UTC string; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, and read call, detect the documented sensor‑absent condition (for example when an I2C read returns the documented error value or fails), handle any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and on a read failure print a diagnostic message to stderr and simply skip that sample, while a SIGINT handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before the program exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors two TI DRV5032 digital Hall‑Effect sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Hall sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Hall sensor 2 to GPIO27 (BCM), configuring both inputs with internal pull‑ups enabled via bias flags, logging the millisecond‑precision timestamped state of each sensor to a file named conveyor_log.txt every 50 ms, and when both sensors read logic 1 the program must simulate halting the conveyor by printing a halt message; the implementation must include robust error handling for all GPIO access operations such as opening the chip, requesting lines, and reading values as well as for file I/O, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources cleanly on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to communicate with an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR IMU, reading the accelerometer and gyroscope X, Y, and Z axes every 100 ms and printing a single line containing the six values to stdout for each sample; the program must check the return value of every I2C operation, handle driver library initialization failure, I2C device open failure, WHO_AM_I register mismatch, any register write failures, and short or failed burst reads by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status, avoid using hard‑coded sleeps that ignore errors, and install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls the appropriate library cleanup function before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens I2C bus 1 on the SDA pin (GPIO2, BCM) and SCL pin (GPIO3, BCM) to communicate with an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board, first confirming the device is present by reading its identification register and comparing the result to the documented value, then initializing the sensor and entering a loop that every 100 ms reads a 12‑byte combined block containing six bytes of 14‑bit left‑aligned accelerometer data followed by six bytes of 16‑bit magnetometer data, extracts the raw X, Y, Z values for both the accelerometer and magnetometer and prints them to the console, while checking each I2C call for errors, retrying on transient read failures, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources—including the I2C handle and any driver state—are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C, evaluates the tilt angle and, whenever the tilt exceeds a threshold of 30.0 degrees, writes a timestamped entry to /var/log/tilt_events.log, performing this sampling and logging cycle every 100 ms; the implementation must include robust error handling that explicitly detects and manages I2C communication failures, sensor‑absent conditions, and bus‑error paths, and must guarantee clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of a Ctrl+C interrupt signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors the digital OUT line of a KY‑038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) over successive 5‑second windows, sampling the pin every 1 ms; after each 5‑second window the program must print to stdout a timestamped line either “ALERT” if the count of high readings exceeds a user‑defined threshold or a status line otherwise, then pause for 1 second before starting the next window, accepting a single command‑line argument that is an integer threshold of minimum high‑readings per window and rejecting any non‑numeric or non‑positive values with a clear error printed to stderr; every call to the GPIO driver API must be checked for failure and any error reported to stderr; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by terminating the driver usage and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that controls two 12 V electromagnetic door locks via TIP120‑driven 5 V active‑HIGH relay modules on the GPIO bus, using GPIO17 (BCM) for Door A and GPIO27 (BCM) for Door B, both initialized as outputs with a default LOW state that keeps the locks energized/closed and a HIGH level that de‑energizes the relay to unlock the door for exactly 5 seconds; at program start and after each successful entry the application must generate a random six‑digit security code in the range 100000‑999999, print it to stdout, then read user input from stdin, handling non‑numeric input by clearing the buffer and re‑prompting, compare the entered code to the generated one, and on a match log a CSV line “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN” to a file named access_log.txt, while printing “Access denied” and continuing on a mismatch; every driver call that opens the chip, gets a line, or requests a line as well as the file open must be checked, with meaningful error messages sent to stderr and a non‑zero exit on any initialization failure; the program must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, and on termination it must set both GPIO outputs to LOW (locking the doors), release all driver resources and close any open file handles; the source must compile with gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3) with the ADDR pin tied to GND, waits up to the maximum 180 ms conversion time, and logs a reading every 5 seconds to a file named light_log.txt using the format “Timestamp: <timestamp>, Lux: <lux_value>”, while handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent (for example failing to open the bus or read bytes), and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) signal.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements an automated plant watering system using two SG90 servo motors controlled via the library's API call, with the valve servo attached to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM) and the nozzle servo attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM); the program must read a simulated soil moisture value that cycles every 1 second through the hard‑coded sequence 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 and, when the moisture is below 50, open the valve by issuing a library's API call with a pulse width corresponding to 90 degrees (≈1500 µs) then sweep the nozzle through the five angles 0, 45, 90, 135 and 180 degrees (pulse widths 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 µs) spending 2 seconds on each step, hold the spray for 5 seconds, close the valve to 0 degrees (500 µs) and then wait 5 seconds before the next cycle, while if the moisture is 50 or above the watering cycle is skipped; every library's API call must have its return value checked, be retried up to three times on failure with a 100 ms backoff and cause the program to exit on unrecoverable error, abort the watering cycle if the valve fails to open, print a critical warning if it fails to close, and log the error but continue to the next angle if a nozzle position fails; the program must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set volatile sig_atomic_t flags, and in the signal handler stop both servos by calling the library's API call with a zero argument, then invoke the library's API call cleanup function and exit cleanly, never invoking any GPIO functions before or after the library's API call in the handler; finally the code should be compiled with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o watering watering.c -lthe driver library -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM) at the documented address, samples the data at 10 Hz, and appends each reading to a file named gyro_log.txt in CSV format containing a timestamp followed by the X, Y, and Z values; the program must check the result of every I2C system call, provide explicit handling for cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that ensure all open file descriptors and any other resources are cleanly released on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives a 28BYJ-48 unipolar stepper motor through an L293D driver to lock and unlock a simulated door on button press, using GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM) for the L293D IN1‑IN4 coil inputs, a LOCK button on GPIO24 (BCM) and an UNLOCK button on GPIO23 (BCM) with internal pull‑ups and active‑low logic, implementing full‑step (single‑coil) excitation and rotating the motor 512 steps clockwise for a LOCK press and 512 steps counter‑clockwise for an UNLOCK press with a 3 ms inter‑step delay, debouncing the button reads so a single press does not trigger multiple rotations, de‑energizing all coils after each rotation to reduce power consumption and heating, printing console messages for lock, unlock and any errors, checking the return value of the library’s API call() after every operation and reporting an error on failure, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) gracefully by de‑energizing the coils and calling the library’s API call() before exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (64‑bit, Bookworm) that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor and logs the result every second to a file named distance_log.txt opened in append mode and kept open for the lifetime of the program; the trigger line must be requested as an output on GPIO17 (BCM) and the echo line as an input on GPIO18 (BCM) with active‑high polarity, the sensor’s 5 V echo output being reduced to 3.3 V by a voltage divider or level shifter before reaching the Pi, the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse, wait for the rising edge of the echo with a 50 ms timeout, then wait for the falling edge with the same timeout, compute the distance, and write the value to the log, pausing at least 60 ms between measurements and sampling at a 1 s interval; on any timeout or driver call failure the program must write “‑1” to the file and print an error message to stderr, and any GPIO initialisation failure must be reported to stderr, while SIGINT or SIGTERM must be caught to cleanly release all driver resources and close the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously simulates a traffic light by cycling four 5V relay modules connected to GPIO17, GPIO22, GPIO23, and GPIO24 (BCM numbering), respecting the sequence red for 10 seconds, red + yellow for 2 seconds, green for 10 seconds, and yellow for 3 seconds before repeating, remembering that the relays are active‑low so a LOW level energizes a relay and a HIGH level turns it off, printing each state transition to stdout, rigorously checking the driver library initialization, chip opening, line request, and every GPIO operation for errors, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that on interruption all GPIO lines are cleanly released before the program exits, while running indefinitely until such a signal is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that simulates a smart greenhouse irrigation system driven by a simulated moisture sensor, using four SainSmart 5V relay modules connected on the GPIO bus with BCM numbering (Relay zone 1 on GPIO4, zone 2 on GPIO17, zone 3 on GPIO27, and zone 4 on GPIO22); the main loop must execute every 5 seconds, generate a random moisture value seeded with time(NULL), treat any reading below 30 as dry soil and activate the corresponding relay by driving the pin LOW (the relays are active‑low), treat readings of 30 or above as wet and deactivate the relay by driving the pin HIGH, and for each iteration append the sensor reading, the resulting ON/OFF state of each relay, and a timestamp to a file named irrigation_log.txt; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, successful opening of the log file, and successful execution of every GPIO operation, and it must install a signal handler for SIGINT (or any error) that deactivates all relays by driving them HIGH, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM 4) using a 100 ms polling interval and, on each rising edge, activates a relay‑controlled 12 V LED floodlight connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM 17) for exactly 60 seconds before turning it off, while appending activation events with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and deactivation events with a timestamp and the measured duration in seconds to a file named security_log.txt; the program must verify that the driver library is successfully initialized, check the return code of every library API call as well as the result of every fopen, fprintf and fclose operation, and if any file operation fails it must turn off the floodlight before exiting, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases the driver library resources, and exits with code 0, ensuring that the floodlight is OFF on all exit paths and that no driver library is used directly in the code.
